title: A polar section on a proper valuation curve with one rational component
statement: Let $K$ be a separably closed [def-kun-separably-closed] field [def-weil-field] and $V\subset K$ a valuation ring with fraction field $K$: for every $a\in K^\times$, either $a$ or $a^{-1}$ lies in $V$. Assume that the prime ideals of $V$ form a finite chain, and put $T=\operatorname{Spec}V$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], with generic point $\eta=\operatorname{Spec}K$. Let $Y$ be a normal proper $T$-curve with geometrically reduced fibres, and let $s$ be the closed point of $T$. Suppose $Z\subset Y_s$ is an irreducible component geometrically isomorphic to a projective line [def-nagata-projective-space-base-change]. Then $Z\simeq\mathbf P^1_{\kappa(s)}$. Assume that $Y_s$ is nodal along $Z$, and that the intersection of $Z$ with the union of the other components consists of at most two transverse branches. No semistability of $Y$ away from $Z$ is assumed. Write $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ for the other irreducible components of $Y_s$ [def-weil-irreducible-components]. There are pairwise disjoint horizontal effective Cartier divisors $P_i\subset Y$ in the relative smooth locus [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], each isomorphic to $T$, such that $(P_i)_s$ is a smooth $\kappa(s)$-rational point $p_i$ of $Z_i$ outside every other component and outside $Z$. For some integer $m>0$, put $P=m\sum_i P_i$ and $L=\mathcal O_Y(P)$ [def-pc-divisor-line-bundle, def-sc-invertible-module]. There exists $a\in\Gamma(Y,L)$ whose value in the one-dimensional fibre $L\otimes\kappa(p_i)$ is nonzero for every $i$. The divisors are effective Cartier in the sense that their ideals are locally generated by one non-zero-divisor; $\mathcal O_Y(P)$ is the dual of that ideal. In a local parameter cutting out $P_i$, the meromorphic function represented by $a$ has pole of order exactly $m$ on the closed fibre at $p_i$ and no poles outside $P$. The canonical section $e=1\in\Gamma(Y,L)$ has zero divisor $P$. The same assertion permits $n=0$, with $P=0$. A $T$-curve means a flat [def-weil-flat-morphism] finitely presented [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation] $T$-scheme of pure relative dimension one [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. A geometric fibre is the base change of a fibre to an algebraic closure of its residue field [def-weil-geometric-fibre]; geometrically reduced means all such fibres have no nonzero nilpotents. An $\eta$-modification is a proper morphism [def-weil-proper-morphism] which is an isomorphism over the generic fibre and over schematically dense open subschemes; schematic density means injectivity of $\mathcal O_Z\to j_*\mathcal O_U$ for the open inclusion. A scheme is normal if every local ring is an integrally closed domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. Its normalization means the scheme obtained by taking the integral closure of its structure sheaf in the product of the function fields of its irreducible components; for an integral scheme this is [def-sc-normalization]. Nodal along $Z$ means that after algebraic closure of the residue field each singularity there has completed local ring $\Omega[[u,v]]/(uv)$ [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion, def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series].

proof.text: Put $k=\kappa(s)$. The valuation ring $V$ is integrally closed: if an element $x$ of $K$ is integral but not in $V$, then $x^{-1}$ is a nonunit of $V$; dividing a monic integral equation by its highest power of $x$ gives $1\in x^{-1}V$, a contradiction. The same argument applies to its localizations. Thus $T$ is integral normal with separably closed function field $K$. Apply [sbc-lem-etale-over-normal] to $T$: its local ring at $s$, namely $V$, is strictly henselian. In particular $V$ is henselian and $k$ is separably closed.

source.place: Temkin Proposition 4.4.6, printed pp. 32--33: polar-section construction; expanded argument

proof.text: The proper component $Z$ becomes $\mathbf P^1$ after extension to an algebraic closure $\overline k$. Smoothness descends by [lem-trf-smooth-fpqc-base-descent]. It has a $k$-rational point $q$ by [lem-pc-rational-points-dense]. The projective-space vanishing [lem-pc-d2-nonnegative-projective-twist-vanishing] and flat cohomology base change [lem-sc-flat-base-change-coherent] give $H^1(Z,\mathcal O_Z)=0$. On the two standard charts of the geometric projective line, a global function lies in both $\overline k[t]$ and $\overline k[t^{-1}]$ inside $\overline k[t,t^{-1}]$, hence is constant. Faithful field extension and the same base-change theorem therefore give $H^0(Z,\mathcal O_Z)=k$. The point $q$ is Cartier by [lem-trf-smooth-curve-section-cartier], applied to $Z\to\operatorname{Spec}k$. By [lem-pc-degree-base-change], $\mathcal O_Z(q)$ has degree one. Apply [lem-trf-pointed-genus-zero-projective-line] to get $Z\simeq\mathbf P^1_k$.

source.place: Temkin Proposition 4.4.6, printed pp. 32--33: polar-section construction; expanded argument

proof.text: If $n=0$, choose $m=1$, $P=0$, $L=\mathcal O_Y$ and $a=e=1$; all point and pole assertions are empty. Hence suppose $n>0$. Write $C=Y_s$ with its reduced structure. Apply [lem-trf-generic-fibre-points-smooth] to $C\to\operatorname{Spec}k$, whose source and base are Noetherian: $C$ is geometrically reduced and of finite type over a field. Around the generic point of each $Z_i$ there is a nonempty smooth open in $C$ disjoint from all other components, including $Z$. By [lem-trf-smooth-at-point-fibre-criterion] these points belong to the relative smooth locus of $Y\to T$, since $Y\to T$ is flat and finitely presented. The rational-point density [lem-pc-rational-points-dense] gives a $k$-rational point $p_i$ in each such open.

source.place: Temkin Proposition 4.4.6, printed pp. 32--33: polar-section construction; expanded argument

proof.text: Choose a smooth affine $T$-neighbourhood $U_i=\operatorname{Spec}B_i$ of $p_i$ inside the relative smooth locus. Its coordinate algebra is smooth over $V$ by the affine smooth-morphism convention. The point is a $V$-algebra map $B_i\to k$. Apply [lem-trf-henselian-smooth-algebra-lifting] with $(A,I)=(V,\mathfrak m_V)$ to obtain $B_i\to V$, hence a section $\sigma_i:T\to Y$ through $p_i$ contained in $U_i$. As $Y\to T$ is separated, [lem-weil-pbc-section-separated-closed-immersion] makes the sections closed immersions. By [lem-trf-smooth-curve-section-cartier] in the smooth locus their images $P_i$ have ideals locally generated by one non-zero-divisor, and the same is true in $Y$ since the ideal is the unit ideal off their images. Two images cannot meet: the inverse image under $\sigma_i$ of the other closed section would be a nonempty closed subset of $T$ and so would contain $s$, contradicting $p_i\ne p_j$. The $P_i$ are therefore pairwise disjoint and each is isomorphic to $T$.

source.place: Temkin Proposition 4.4.6, printed pp. 32--33: polar-section construction; expanded argument

proof.text: Let $E=\sum_i p_i$ on $C$, $W=\bigcup_i Z_i$ with reduced structure, and $D=Z\cap W$ with its scheme-theoretic structure. The points $p_i$ are smooth points of $C$ and $W$, so $E$ is Cartier on both; write $\mathcal I_D$ for the ideal of $D$ in $W$. For $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}$ put $N_{m,\epsilon}=\mathcal O_C(mE-\epsilon E)$. Because $E$ is disjoint from $Z$, restriction to $Z$ has a canonical trivialization. There is an exact sequence on $C$, with $j_W,j_Z$ the closed inclusions, $0\to j_{W,*}(\mathcal I_D\otimes\mathcal O_W((m-\epsilon)E))\to N_{m,\epsilon}\to j_{Z,*}\mathcal O_Z\to0$. Indeed, on an affine open with component ideals $I$ for $Z$ and $J$ for $W$, reducedness of $C=Z\cup W$ says $I\cap J=0$. The kernel $I$ of $A\to A/I$ identifies with $(I+J)/J$, the ideal of $D$ in $W$. Tensor this identity with the locally free rank-one module $N_{m,\epsilon}$. This proves the sequence without any hypothesis on the singularities away from $Z$.

source.place: Temkin Proposition 4.4.6, printed pp. 32--33: polar-section construction; expanded argument

proof.text: Put $M=\mathcal O_W(E)$. On each normalized irreducible component of $W$, the pullback of the canonical section of $M$ is nonzero and has a zero above $p_i$: near $p_i$ the curve is smooth and the divisor is its reduced rational point. Thus its degree is positive by [lem-trf-curve-section-degree-positivity]; pullback preserves invertibility by [lem-weil-pbc-invertible-pullback-tensor]. The componentwise degree criterion [lem-trf-fibre-degree-ample-criterion] shows that $M$ is ample on the proper reduced curve $W$. The two fixed coherent sheaves $\mathcal I_D$ and $\mathcal I_D\otimes M^{-1}$ may have singular support; Serre vanishing applies to coherent sheaves, so no smoothness or semistability of $W$ is needed.

source.place: Temkin Proposition 4.4.6, printed pp. 32--33: polar-section construction; expanded argument

proof.text: Apply [lem-pc-serre-vanishing] to those two coherent sheaves and $M$. For one sufficiently large positive $m$, both $H^1(W,\mathcal I_D\otimes M^m)$ and $H^1(W,\mathcal I_D\otimes M^{m-1})$ vanish. The closed-immersion cohomology comparison [lem-sc-cohomology-closed-immersion-pushforward], together with [lem-sc-zariski-module-abelian-cohomology-agree], identifies these with the cohomology of their direct images on $C$. The long exact sequence of right derived global sections [lem-weil-pbc-right-derived-universal-delta-functor] for the two sequences in step 5, and $H^1(Z,\mathcal O_Z)=0$, give $H^1(C,\mathcal O_C(mE))=H^1(C,\mathcal O_C(mE-E))=0$.

source.place: Temkin Proposition 4.4.6, printed pp. 32--33: polar-section construction; expanded argument

proof.text: The evaluation sequence $0\to\mathcal O_C(mE-E)\to\mathcal O_C(mE)\to\mathcal O_C(mE)|_E\to0$ is exact, as is seen by dividing by a local parameter at each $p_i$. Its section boundary has zero target by step 7. By [lem-sc-module-section-boundary-exact], every section on $E$ lifts to $C$. Each fibre over $p_i$ is one-dimensional over $k$, so choose a nonzero vector in each of these finitely many fibres. Their tuple lifts to $a_s\in H^0(C,\mathcal O_C(mE))$, and $a_s(p_i)\ne0$ for all $i$.

source.place: Temkin Proposition 4.4.6, printed pp. 32--33: polar-section construction; expanded argument

proof.text: Put $P=m\sum_iP_i$ and $L=\mathcal O_Y(P)$. Locally its ideal is $(t^m)$ and its dual is generated by $t^{-m}$, so $L$ is invertible, flat over $V$ because $Y$ is flat, and of finite presentation as an $\mathcal O_Y$-module. The quotient $\mathcal O_{P_i}\simeq\mathcal O_T$ is $V$-flat, so tensoring its ideal sequence with $k$ preserves injectivity. The resulting ideal cuts out $p_i$; its generator is a local parameter there, since the fibre section is a smooth curve point. Thus restriction gives $L_s=\mathcal O_C(mE)$. Cohomology above degree one on $C$ vanishes by [lem-sc-noetherian-cohomology-above-dimension]. Combining this with step 7 gives $H^q(C,L_s)=0$ for every $q\ne0$. Its degree-zero cohomology is finite-dimensional by [lem-pc-coherent-hi]. Apply the general form of [sk-thm-picard-perfect] with $i=0$ and $r=\dim_kH^0(C,L_s)$. Its open locus contains $s$ and therefore is all of $T$, since an open neighbourhood of the closed point of a local spectrum is the whole spectrum. Consequently $f_*L$ is finite locally free and formation of $H^0$ commutes with the base change to $s$. Since $T$ is affine, $\Gamma(Y,L)\otimes_V k\simeq H^0(C,L_s)$; quotienting a module by $\mathfrak m_V$ is surjective. Lift $a_s$ to $a\in\Gamma(Y,L)$.

source.place: Temkin Proposition 4.4.6, printed pp. 32--33: polar-section construction; expanded argument

proof.text: The local generator $t$ of the ideal of $P_i$ restricts to a uniformizer of the smooth point $p_i$ on $C$. Write $a=b\,t^{-m}$ locally. The assertion $a_s(p_i)\ne0$ says $b(p_i)\ne0$, so $b$ is a unit near $p_i$ and its restriction to $C$ is a unit in the corresponding local ring. Thus the associated meromorphic function has pole order exactly $m$ at $p_i$. Away from $P$, the inclusion $L\subseteq\mathcal K_Y$ is just $\mathcal O_Y\subseteq\mathcal K_Y$, so there are no other poles; this inclusion is defined by inverting the non-zero-divisor $t$. Finally $e=1$ is locally $t^m\,t^{-m}$, hence its zero scheme is exactly $P$. The lifted value at each $p_i$ is the selected nonzero vector. These are all the required conclusions.
